scenario: WIBTA for testing my boyfriend? | So a short backstory on me, I am a model. And with that most of my previous relationships stem from the guys I am dating on really dating me because of my looks and the "status symbol" of dating a model not because of me as a person. This is something that has caused a lot of anxiety and depression in my life and I have been really trying to find people in my life that care about me not what I look like. Now that is not to say that my looks can't play a role (physical attraction is important to me as well) but I can't be with anyone where that is the only or main reason why they are dating me. So that brings me to a guy a started dating fairly recently. I really like him and he seems like a good guy. Takes interest in my hobbies and is supportive of what I do. He enjoys lazy days around the house and cooking for me at home instead of always wanting to go out (which with a lot of guys it just seemed like they wanted to show me off). So I really really like him. But his friend DM'd me the other day and told me, "Hey, just thought you should know. You boyfriend has been telling anyone who will listen about all the dirty shit he gets to do with 'this model chick I have been banging'. I'd want to know. Hope for the best!" I have only met this guy once and I don't know how close he is to my boyfriend nor do I know why he told me this. For all I know he is just trying to start drama. The problem is I know how badly I want to believe my boyfriend. And if he were to tell me that it isn't true I would probably believe him. But that thought of "what if" would constantly be in my head from now on. So would I be an asshole if for the next month or so I stop wearing makeup when we go out and I don't put out at all (just come up with whatever excuse I need to when he starts trying to make a move)? If I test what his motives truly are? Part of me feels like this is wrong but the other part knows this is the only way I can fully 100% put this behind me. And if his friend is lying I can commit to him 100%

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

While your intent is to uncover his true motives, the *method* could: - Make you feel like you’re "proving" something rather than building trust. - Create a power dynamic where you’re controlling the interaction to "test" him, which might not reflect how you’d behave in a healthy relationship. - Lead to him feeling **insecure, confused, or even resentful** if he later finds out about the test (even if he passes it). - If he *does* react poorly (e.g., gets angry, accuses you of being cold), you’ll have to deal with the fallout of a relationship that may already be strained by this revelation. 3. **The Friend’s Role: Uncertainty and Bias** - You don’t know the friend’s **motives** (is he trying to start drama? Is he genuinely concerned? Is he jealous?). This adds a layer of ambiguity. If the friend is lying or exaggerating, your test could backfire. - Even if the friend’s claim is true, **words ≠ actions**. Testing him could either: - **Help you move forward** by confirming his sincerity (if he passes the test). - **Reinforce your fear** that people only care about your looks, even if he’s genuinely different. - Alternatively, you could **focus on rebuilding trust** without the test. For example: - Have an **honest conversation** with him about your concerns (e.g., *"I’ve had past experiences where guys only saw me as a status symbol. I want to make sure you’re different. Can you help me understand where you’re coming from?"*). - **Observe his actions over time** (does he treat you like a person, not an object? Does he respect your boundaries?). - **Consider whether this is a dealbreaker**—if his friend’s claim is true, would you be able to move on from it? 5. **The "What If" Trap** - The fear of "what if" is real, but **dwelling on it** can create a self-fulfilling prophecy. If you assume he’s not genuine until proven otherwise, you might **miss out on a real connection** because you’re too busy testing him. - On the other hand, **assuming he’s genuine without evidence** could lead to heartbreak if he’s not. --- ### **Alternative Approaches** Instead of testing him, consider these steps: 1. **Ask Directly (But Carefully)** - Frame it as a **curiosity about his perspective**, not an accusation. For example: > *"I’ve noticed some guys in the past have talked about me in ways that made me feel like they only saw me as a status symbol. I want to make sure that’s not the case with us. Can you tell me how you’ve talked about me to others?"* - This gives him a chance to **clarify his intentions** without you having to "prove" anything. 2. **Watch His Reactions** - Does he **defend you** when others talk about you? Does he **respect your boundaries** (e.g., not pressuring you for photos, not making you feel like an object)? Does he **engage with you as a person**, not just your appearance? - If he’s genuinely different, his actions will show over time. 3. **Therapy or Self-Reflection** - If this is a **deep-seated fear**, working with a therapist could help you **process past trauma** and **build healthier relationship patterns**. Testing someone out of fear might not lead to the security you’re seeking. 4. **Gray Rock Method (If You’re Unsure)** - If you’re not ready to confront him but want to **avoid drama**, you could **minimize interaction** with the friend who messaged you (blocking or ignoring them) and **focus on your boyfriend’s behavior**. This reduces the risk of escalation. --- ### **Final Verdict: Would You Be an Asshole?** - **Yes, in some ways.** Testing him by withholding intimacy and appearance could feel like **gaslighting** or **controlling** him, even if your intent is good. It puts the burden on *him* to "prove" himself, which isn’t a healthy dynamic. - **No, if you frame it as a conversation.** If you approach this as a **shared discussion about trust and boundaries** (rather than a test), it could actually **strengthen your relationship** if he’s secure enough to handle it. --- ### **What I’d Recommend** Given your history and emotions, I’d suggest: 1. **Don’t test him.** Instead, **have an open conversation** about your concerns. This shows you trust him enough to be vulnerable. 2. **Observe his actions.** Does he treat you like a person? Does he respect your boundaries? 3. **Consider whether this is a red flag.** If his friend’s claim is true, would you be able to move on? If not, you might need to **walk away** to protect your peace. 4. **Focus on rebuilding trust.** If he’s genuinely different, he’ll **earn your belief** through consistency, not through you "proving" him. --- ### **Bottom Line** This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **what will lead to the healthiest outcome for you**. Testing him could give you answers, but it might cost you more than it’s worth. **Trust is built through communication, not manipulation.** If you can’t have that conversation without testing him, it might be a sign that he’s not the right person for you.
